title: Strengthening Sovereignty in the North Natuna Sea: An Evaluation of Indonesia's Maritime Security and Deterrence Strategy
content:
### Abstract

> This study aims to analyze the dynamics of maritime security threats and evaluate the effectiveness of Indonesia's deterrence strategy in the North Natuna Sea against China's grey-zone tactics and transnational maritime crimes. Using a descriptive qualitative approach based on library research, secondary data were gathered from official government reports, the UNCLOS 1982 legal framework, and academic literature. The findings reveal that Indonesia's sovereignty and sovereign rights in the North Natuna Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) are continually challenged by coercive actions from the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the proliferation of dark vessels. These external vulnerabilities are exacerbated by domestic structural issues, including jurisdictional fragmentation among seven ministries/agencies lacking a single command system, operational inefficiencies in patrol fuel allocation, and a physical vacuum in the EEZ due to the dominance of micro-scale local fishing fleets (<5 GT). The study concludes that enhancing Indonesia's deterrence effect requires comprehensive maritime governance reform, focusing on establishing a unified command regulation under Bakamla RI, integrating maritime intelligence surveillance technology (smart power), and mobilizing local fishing fleets (>30 GT) as economic drivers and civilian early warning systems (soft power) along the border.

**Keywords:** `#Bakamla` `#Deterrence Strategy` `#Grey-Zone Tactics` `#Maritime Security` `#North Natuna Sea.`

---


## 1.

Introduction

 

### 1.1 Background & Strategic Significance

 The North Natuna Sea is a strategic body of water holding vital economic, geopolitical, and security value for Indonesia (CNN Indonesia, 2016; Kemenko Polkam RI, 2023). Under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS 1982), Indonesia holds sovereign rights over the exploration and exploitation of natural resources within its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and continental shelf (United Nations, 1982).

Although Indonesia has consistently maintained its position as a non-claimant state in the South China Sea territorial disputes, its sovereignty and sovereign rights face continuous friction from the unilateral Nine-Dash Line claim asserted by the People's Republic of China (PRC) (Fanani et al., 2026; KIARA, 2023). China systematically employs Grey-Zone Warfare deploying the China Coast Guard (CCG) and maritime militia forces to enforce historical claims without triggering open military conflict (Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, 2023; Forum Sinologi Indonesia, 2025).

Security dynamics in the North Natuna Sea have evolved beyond conventional territorial boundary disputes into transnational maritime crime threats (Agnew & Barnes, 2004; Ruang Kota, 2025). Maritime surveillance gaps are evidenced by rampant Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (IUU) Fishing and the intrusion of dark vessels foreign ships that intentionally deactivate their Automatic Identification System (AIS) (Asnawi, 2026; Ismail et al., 2018).

Daily transit records peaked at 1,647 vessels in April 2019 and maintained an average of 315 vessels per day in late 2024, highlighting significant gaps in national maritime surveillance (CNN Indonesia, 2020, 2024b). These vulnerabilities are compounded by illicit ship-to-ship crude oil transfers, such as the MT Arman 114 tanker case in 2023 (Calista et al., 2026), and direct interferences by CCG 5402 harassing 3D seismic surveys conducted by PT Pertamina’s MV Geo Coral in October 2024 (Damarjati, 2024; Tempo, 2024).

In International Relations and maritime security studies, Indonesia's deterrence failure in the North Natuna Sea stems not only from external coercive pressure but also from domestic structural anomalies in maritime governance (Fanani et al., 2026; Rohana, 2021). Indonesia suffers from acute institutional fragmentation, with at least seven ministries and agencies holding operational mandates at sea without a unified single command system (Chairijah, 2005; Kemenko Polkam RI, 2023).

Inter-agency rivalries are further exacerbated by fuel logistics inefficiencies, the enforcement of a "docking strategy" due to patrol budget constraints, and a physical vacuum of presence in the outer EEZ caused by the overwhelming dominance of micro-scale local fishing vessels under 5 Gross Tons (GT) (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2025; Dinas Perikanan Kabupaten Natuna, 2024; Satu Data Natuna, 2026).

This mismatch between regional asymmetric threats and national maritime enforcement capabilities erodes Indonesia's deterrence posture across Southeast Asia and China. Research Questions Based on the background above, this study addresses the following research questions: 1. How do grey-zone threats and transnational maritime crimes impact Indonesia's sovereignty and sovereign rights in the North Natuna Sea?

2. What structural and operational impediments in Indonesia's maritime security governance undermine its deterrence strategy along the maritime border? 3.

What ideal policy reform strategies should be implemented to bolster Indonesia's deterrence posture and sovereignty in the North Natuna Sea? METHOD This study employs a descriptive-qualitative research design to evaluate maritime security dynamics and measure the effectiveness of Indonesia's deterrence strategy in the North Natuna Sea. A qualitative approach was selected for its capacity to provide in-depth analytical insights into complex international political phenomena, particularly regarding grey-zone tactics, territorial confrontations, and domestic institutional governance dynamics (Fanani et al., 2026).

Data collection was conducted through library research, leveraging secondary data categorized into three primary clusters: ● International Legal Documents and Policy Frameworks: UNCLOS 1982 legal frameworks (United Nations, 1982), the 2016 Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) ruling, China's 2021 Coast Guard Law, and Indonesian national maritime regulations (Badan Pembinaan Hukum Nasional, 2005). ● Operational Data and Institutional Reports: Official performance reports of the Indonesian Maritime Security Agency (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2024, 2025, 2026), vessel transit logs from the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries (Direktorat Jenderal PSDKP, 2025a, 2025b), crisis incident reports from the Indonesian Navy Information Center (Pusat Penerangan TNI, 2024; TNI Angkatan Laut, 2024), and AIS traffic logs from Bakamla's Natuna Station. ● Academic Literature and Verified Media Records: Peer-reviewed journal articles (Calista et al., 2026; Fanani et al., 2026; Rohana, 2021), policy analyses from think tanks such as the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative / CSIS (Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, 2023), and verified investigative media reports (BBC News Indonesia, 2020; CNBC Indonesia, 2020; Kompas.com, 2021).

Data analysis was executed using qualitative content analysis and documentary analysis techniques. Data validity was maintained through source triangulation, cross-referencing field incident reports with satellite surveillance data and established international legal norms. Synthesized data were analyzed using maritime security conceptual frameworks and classical deterrence theory to identify policy gaps and formulate actionable strategy projections. 

## 4.

Results and Discussion

 1. External Threat Dynamics: China's Grey-Zone Tactics and Transnational Maritime Crime Security escalation in the North Natuna Sea no longer manifests primarily as conventional military invasion, shifting instead toward Grey-Zone Warfare tactics. China leverages its historical Nine-Dash Line claim, which directly overlaps with Indonesia's legitimate EEZ boundaries under UNCLOS 1982 (United Nations, 1982; Fanani et al., 2026).

Within this grey-zone framework, China combines non-military assets, such as the China Coast Guard (CCG) and maritime militia fleets to enforce jurisdictional claims while avoiding open armed conflict (Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, 2023; Forum Sinologi Indonesia, 2025). The harassment of PT Pertamina East Natuna's MV Geo Coral from October 19 to 24, 2024, exemplifies this strategy (CNN Indonesia, 2024a; Damarjati, 2024).

While the vessel was carrying out a 3D Arwana seismic survey within Indonesia's continental shelf, CCG 5402 actively intercepted and maneuvered provocatively. Shadowing operations conducted by Bakamla's KN Tanjung Datu-301, KN Pulau Dana-323, and the Indonesian Navy's KRI Sutedi Senaputera 378 successfully repelled the vessel, demonstrating China's systematic attempts to disrupt national strategic projects to force de facto recognition of its claims (Pusat Penerangan TNI, 2024; Tempo, 2024; TNI Angkatan Laut, 2024).

Threat Parameter Manifestation in the North Natuna Sea Implications for Indonesia Grey-Zone Intrusions CCG 5402 and maritime militia deployment harassing offshore oil and gas exploration (MV Geo Coral, Oct 2024) (Damarjati, 2024; Tempo, 2024). Challenges sovereign rights over exclusive resources and threatens national energy security (Kompas.com, 2021).

Dark Vessels & IUU Fishing 1,533 foreign vessels deactivated AIS in April 2019; averaging 315 vessel transits/day in Oct 2024 (CNN Indonesia, 2020, 2024b). Fiscal losses, marine ecosystem degradation, and erosion of economic sovereignty (Mahabror & Hidayat, 2018; Ruang Kota, 2025). Transnational Crime Illicit ship-to-ship crude oil transfers by Iranian-flagged tanker MT Arman 114 in Vulnerability of the Indonesian EEZ as a safe haven for international 2023 (Calista et al., 2026). criminal syndicates (Calista et al., 2026).

Surveillance blind spots along border zones are exploited by transnational crime syndicates (Agnew & Barnes, 2004). Vessel monitoring data indicates high volumes of dark vessel traffic deactivating AIS units to evade detection (CNN Indonesia, 2020). Cases involving illegal ship-to-ship oil transfers by MT Arman 114 in 2023 and the detention of foreign trawl fleets, such as Vietnamese-flagged vessels intercepted by KKP in November 2025 demonstrate that the North Natuna Sea remains exposed to transnational crime due to suboptimal national patrol capacity (Calista et al., 2026; Direktorat Jenderal PSDKP, 2025b; Kementerian Kelautan dan Perikanan, 2025).

2. Internal Problematics: Institutional Fragmentation and Operational Deficits External security challenges are exacerbated by structural anomalies in Indonesia's domestic maritime architecture, primarily institutional fragmentation (Chairijah, 2005). At present, seven distinct ministries and agencies hold operational mandates at sea, including the Indonesian Navy (TNI AL), Bakamla, PSDKP-KKP, Maritime Police (Polairud), Customs (Bea Cukai), the Ministry of Transportation (Hubla), and the National Anti-Narcotics Agency (BNN) (Kemenko Polkam RI, 2023; Rohana, 2021).

The absence of a single command system generates inter-agency rivalries, jurisdictional overlaps, and bureaucratic delays in operational response times. These structural impediments are compounded by two critical operational bottlenecks: ● Logistical Inefficiencies and Fuel Budget Deficits: High operational fuel requirements reaching 14–15 tons of fuel per vessel per day, restrict the Indonesian Navy to deploying an average of 5 warships (KRIs) out of a minimum baseline requirement of 8 KRIs (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2025; BPH Migas, 2026).

Similarly, Bakamla relies on a "docking strategy" (retaining vessels in port), maintaining only 3–4 active patrol craft out of an ideal deployment requirement of 9–10 vessels in Natuna waters (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2024, 2026). ● Physical Vacuum of Presence ( Vacuum of Presence ): Local fishing fleets in Natuna Regency remain heavily dominated by micro-scale vessels under 5 Gross Tons (GT) (Dinas Perikanan Kabupaten Natuna, 2021, 2024; Satu Data Natuna, 2026).

Because these vessels have an operational range limited to approximately 20 nautical miles from the coast, outer EEZ areas remain de facto empty of domestic civilian presence (BBC News Indonesia, 2020; Mongabay Indonesia, 2025). Foreign fishing vessels and Chinese coast guard assets readily occupy this physical vacuum. 3.

Evaluation of Deterrence Posture and Indonesia's Maritime Policy Projections Under classical deterrence theory, an effective deterrence posture requires three core elements: capability , credibility , and communication (Fanani et al., 2026). Indonesia's inability to maintain a persistent patrol presence and resolve internal inter-agency friction has weakened its deterrence credibility in the eyes of China and neighboring Southeast Asian states.

Maintaining the status quo ( worst-case scenario ) risks a gradual loss of economic sovereignty across the EEZ, the halting of strategic offshore energy projects due to recurring harassment, and unmitigated resource exploitation (Bloomberg Technoz, 2025; Mahabror & Hidayat, 2018; Ruang Kota, 2025). Consequently, maritime policy reform must focus on three strategic pillars: ● Unified Command Regulation ( Single Agency Command ): Issuing a Presidential Instruction (Inpres) designating Bakamla as the sole agency holding operational command for maritime law enforcement to streamline inter-agency operations and eliminate sectoral silos (Kemenko Polkam RI, 2023; Rohana, 2021). ● Enhancing Smart Power (Radar & Satellite Integration): Consolidating maritime intelligence surveillance networks across Bakamla, the Navy, and KKP to detect dark vessels and monitor CCG movements in real-time (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2025). ● Mobilizing Local EEZ Fishermen as Soft Power : Reallocating fuel subsidies and providing vessel assistance (>30 GT steel/wooden trawlers) to domestic fishing cooperatives (Leader Nusantara, 2021; Serayu Nusantara, 2026).

Establishing a permanent civilian presence along border zones serves a dual purpose as an economic driver and a civilian early warning system filling the physical vacuum in the North Natuna EEZ (VOA Indonesia, 2020). 

## 5. Conclusion and Policy Recommendations

 Resolving boundary friction and securing the North Natuna Sea can no longer be approached purely as conventional border governance; it represents a complex maritime security environment marked by China's Grey-Zone Warfare and transnational maritime crimes (Agnew & Barnes, 2004; Fanani et al., 2026).

The findings demonstrate that Indonesia's sovereignty and sovereign rights within its Exclusive Economic Zone are repeatedly challenged by China Coast Guard intrusions and AIS-evading dark vessels (Calista et al., 2026; Damarjati, 2024). These external threats are exacerbated by internal structural vulnerabilities, including fragmented command structures among seven agencies, operational patrol fuel constraints, and an physical vacuum of domestic civilian presence in the outer EEZ (Badan Keamanan Laut Republik Indonesia, 2025; Rohana, 2021; Satu Data Natuna, 2026).

To restore and solidify its deterrence posture along its Southeast Asian and Chinese maritime borders, Indonesia must shift from reactive diplomatic protests toward integrated structural reform (Kemenko Polkam RI, 2023). This requires enacting a unified single command regulation under Bakamla RI, integrating satellite-based smart power surveillance networks, and mobilizing local fishing fleets (>30 GT) as soft power assets serving both economic and civilian early warning functions across the North Natuna Exclusive Economic Zone (Serayu Nusantara, 2026; VOA Indonesia, 2020).
